coordinates.precisionLabel: Loch Ness deep basin (57.32° N, 4.42° W)

mysteries.imageAlt: The Loch Ness Monster — archival editorial visual plate

overview.what: Folklore and reported sightings of a large long-necked aquatic animal ("Nessie") inhabiting Scotland’s deepest freshwater volume loch.
overview.where: Loch Ness, Inverness-shire, Scottish Highlands.
overview.when: Modern media wave began in 1933; 1934 Surgeon’s Photo confessed hoax in 1994; eDNA survey published 2019.
overview.narrative: Loch Ness holds more fresh water than all lakes in England and Wales combined, plunging 230 meters through dark peat-stained water. Yet a breeding population of giant marine reptiles requires dozens of individuals, visible surface air-breathing every few minutes, and a massive fish food base—none of which exist in the cold, nutrient-poor loch. In 2019, geneticist Neil Gemmell filtered 250 water samples across every depth and found no reptile or monster DNA—only normal fish, birds, and remarkably widespread European eel DNA.

whyMysterious: Why do surface boat wakes, floating logs, diving birds, and large eels continue creating persuasive optical illusions on misty Highland water?

timeline.title: The "Surgeon’s Photograph" Published
timeline.description: Most famous Nessie photo runs in the Daily Mail—later revealed as a toy submarine with plastic wood neck.
timeline.significance: Shaped global visual image of Nessie.

timeline.title: Operation Deepscan & BBC Sonar
timeline.description: Full-width sonar sweeps detect no large unknown pelagic animals.
timeline.significance: Ruled out a large breeding colony.

timeline.title: University of Otago eDNA Survey
timeline.description: 250 samples sequenced across Loch Ness find zero plesiosaur or sturgeon sequences, but dense eel DNA.

whatWeKnow: Loch Ness formed only ~10,000 years ago after the last Ice Age—far too young to trap 66-million-year-old Mesozoic plesiosaurs.
Christian Spurling confessed in 1994 that the 1934 photo used a 14-inch toy submarine.
The 2019 eDNA study ruled out plesiosaurs, giant catfish, and Greenland sharks.

mysteries.finalAssessment: The Loch Ness Monster is beloved Scottish folklore unsupported by sonar, ecology, or environmental DNA.

mysteries.title: The Himalayan Yeti
mysteries.subtitle: Mountaineering footprints and 2017 DNA sequencing of purported Yeti relics
mysteries.summary: For a century, giant footprints in Himalayan snow fueled tales of an "Abominable Snowman"—until 2017 DNA sequencing of nine Yeti relics traced them to Himalayan bears and a dog.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: Peer-reviewed 2017 mitochondrial DNA sequencing of nine museum and monastery "Yeti" hair, bone, and skin samples identified 8 as Himalayan/Tibetan brown and black bears and 1 as a dog, refuting an unknown ape.

overview.what: Folklore and mountaineer reports of an upright ape-like creature ("Meh-teh" / Yeti) inhabiting snowbound Himalayan passes.
overview.where: Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan, and northern India.
overview.when: Western publicity peaked with Eric Shipton’s 1951 Menlung footprint photo; DNA resolved in 2017.
overview.narrative: In 1951, British mountaineer Eric Shipton photographed huge tracks at 5,800 meters in the Menlung Basin. Decades of searches followed, yet no verified skeleton, scat, or living primate ever turned up above the snowline. In 2017, geneticist Charlotte Lindqvist sequenced mitochondrial genomes from nine purported Yeti bones, teeth, skins, and hairs kept in monasteries and private collections—matching every single one to native Himalayan brown bears, Tibetan brown bears, Asian black bears, or domestic dogs.

whyMysterious: How do sun-melted bear tracks in snow fool experienced mountaineers into seeing giant human-like footprints?

whatWeKnow: When bears walk, hind feet step directly into front-paw prints, and midday sun melting enlarges edges into single giant "humanoid" tracks.
All 9 biological relics tested in 2017 belonged to known bears (Ursus arctos isabellinus, Ursus thibetanus) or dogs.
In Sherpa tradition, the Yeti is closely intertwined with spiritual folklore and rare sightings of the endangered Himalayan brown bear.

mysteries.finalAssessment: The Himalayan Yeti is rooted in genuine Sherpa folklore and rare encounters with endangered Himalayan bears—not an undiscovered bipedal ape.

overview.when: Active March 1952 – December 1969 (covering records back to 1947).
overview.narrative: Tasked with assessing whether aerial sightings posed a national security threat or involved unknown technology, Air Force investigators logged 12,618 reports. Astronomical consultant J. overview.what: Top-secret 1947 U.S. Army Air Forces program launching long trains of weather balloons carrying microphones to listen for Soviet nuclear tests.

overview.when: Mogul Flight 4 launched June 4, 1947; debris found mid-June and reported July 8, 1947.
overview.narrative: Because Project Mogul was classified as high-priority nuclear intelligence in 1947, Roswell base officers could not reveal what rancher Mac Brazel had found on his pasture—leading to an infamous confused press release mentioning a "flying disc," quickly corrected hours later to a weather balloon. When the 1995 USAF report released NYU scientist Charles Moore’s flight logs, the exotic pink-and-purple tape symbols turned out to be ordinary toy-factory adhesive tape used on balsa-and-foil Rawin radar reflectors.

whyMysterious: Why did a 1947 cover story meant to hide nuclear-detection balloons spark the world’s most famous alien crash legend 30 years later?

mysteries.evidenceRationale: The Nizari Ismaili state at Alamut (1090–1256) and Hasan-i Sabbah’s asymmetric strategy are verified by Persian chronicles and archaeology, while Western tales of drugged paradise gardens are unsupported medieval propaganda.

overview.when: 1090 CE (seizure of Alamut) – 1256 CE (Mongol conquest by Hulagu Khan).
overview.narrative: Surrounded by vast Seljuk and Crusader empires, the smaller Nizari Ismaili community survived for 166 years by defending nearly impregnable mountain peaks and dispatching elite "fida’is" to eliminate rival rulers in public—avoiding mass battlefield slaughter. Hostile Sunni and Crusader chroniclers nicknamed them "Hashishiyya" (a derogatory slang insult meaning "outcasts/lowlifes"), inspiring Marco Polo’s fanciful tale of drugged assassins in secret gardens.

whyMysterious: How much of the Alamut library and real Nizari doctrine survived the 1256 Mongol destruction?

Alamut housed an astronomical observatory, hydraulic cisterns, and a major philosophical library.
The English word "assassin" entered European languages directly from medieval Crusader encounters with the Syrian Nizaris.

mysteries.subtitle: 129 sailors lost in the Northwest Passage—and the 2014–2016 discovery of Erebus and Terror
mysteries.summary: Sir John Franklin’s two Royal Navy ships vanished into the Canadian Arctic in 1845; guided by Inuit oral history, Parks Canada located both remarkably preserved wrecks beneath Arctic ice.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: The tragic fate of the expedition (ships beset in ice near King William Island, Victory Point Note, crew starvation/scurvy/exposure, and wrecks of HMS Erebus and Terror) is verified by archaeology and DNA, though exact leadership breakdown details remain studied.

overview.what: 1845 British Arctic naval expedition aboard HMS Erebus and HMS Terror seeking the Northwest Passage; all 129 officers and crew perished.
overview.where: Victoria Strait and King William Island, Nunavut, Canadian Arctic.
overview.when: Sailed May 1845; abandoned ships April 1848; wrecks discovered September 2014 & September 2016.
overview.narrative: Equipped with steam engines, reinforced hulls, and three years of tinned provisions, Franklin’s expedition appeared invincible. Yet Victoria Strait pack ice trapped both ships from September 1846 through April 1848, when Captain Francis Crozier left a brief note in a stone cairn recording Franklin’s death and a desperate march south toward Back’s Fish River. Over 160 years later, Inuit oral testimonies led Parks Canada sonar teams straight to both sunken hulls sitting upright on the icy seabed.

whyMysterious: How much did botulism, scurvy, pneumonia, or zinc/lead deficiency accelerate the crew’s collapse during the 1848 ice march?

timeline.significance: Documented in the Victory Point Note.

timeline.title: HMS Erebus & HMS Terror Wrecks Found

whatWeKnow: Inuit oral histories faithfully preserved the ships’ locations and crew encounters for 160 years.

2018–2021 synchrotron X-ray and DNA studies showed lead levels from soldered tins were no higher than typical 19th-century sailors—pointing instead to scurvy, tuberculosis, zinc deficiency, and starvation.
Cut marks on skeletal bones from King William Island confirm desperate end-stage survival cannibalism.

scientificInvestigation.narrative: Combining Indigenous geographical memory with modern underwater robotics solved the locations of both lost Victorian ships.

whatRemainsUnknown: Written officer logs that may still survive inside sealed drawers aboard HMS Terror.
mysteries.finalAssessment: The Franklin Expedition’s broad fate is verified and deeply poignant—with ongoing underwater archaeology still uncovering personal diaries beneath the Arctic sea.

mysteries.evidenceRationale: Superintendent Robert Muirhead’s December 1900 inspection report verifies the missing men and violent storm damage at the west landing, yet with no bodies or eyewitnesses, the exact fatal sequence remains unresolved.

overview.when: Vanished around December 15, 1900; discovered December 26, 1900.
overview.narrative: Popular poems and retellings later invented "phantom overturned chairs," "half-eaten meals," and eerie final logbook entries about weeping men—none of which appear in the actual 1900 Northern Lighthouse Board report! Superintendent Muirhead’s primary investigation found the kitchen tidy, lamps trimmed, one set of oilskins left indoors, and massive storm destruction 33 meters above sea level at the west landing stage—concluding a rogue Atlantic wave swept the men away while securing equipment.

Donald McArthur’s oilskins were still on their peg, suggesting he rushed out in shirtsleeves to warn or rescue his two colleagues.

mysteries.finalAssessment: While no bodies were recovered, primary lighthouse inspection records strongly point to a tragic rogue-wave accident rather than supernatural mystery.

mysteries.title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke
mysteries.subtitle: 115 English settlers, the word "CROATOAN," and Hatteras Island archaeology
mysteries.summary: When Governor John White returned to Roanoke Island in 1590 after a war-delayed supply trip, his 115 colonists were gone—leaving dismantled houses and "CROATOAN" carved into a post.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: The 1590 abandonment and "CROATOAN" inscription are verified historical records, and Hatteras archaeology points toward integration with Indigenous Croatoan communities, though final proof of the colonists’ fate remains unresolved.

coordinates.precisionLabel: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site (35.94° N, 75.71° W)

overview.what: England’s 1587 attempt to establish a permanent settlement on Roanoke Island, whose 115 men, women, and children vanished before 1590.
overview.where: Roanoke Island and nearby Outer Banks / Albemarle Sound, North Carolina.
overview.when: Founded July 1587; found abandoned August 18, 1590.
overview.narrative: Before Governor White sailed back to England for supplies in 1587, he agreed with the settlers that if they relocated, they would carve their destination—and add a cross if leaving under distress. When White returned three years later after the Spanish Armada blockade, he found the houses neatly taken down, a palisade built, and "CROATOAN" clearly carved with no distress cross. Modern excavations at nearby Hatteras Island (Croatoan) uncovered 16th-century English rapier hilts, slate pencils, and copper alongside Native pottery.

whyMysterious: Did the colonists split into groups—some joining the friendly Croatoan on Hatteras Island while others moved 50 miles inland toward "Site X" on Bertie County’s Chowan River?

whatWeKnow: No cross was carved above "CROATOAN"—the pre-arranged signal indicating voluntary relocation rather than attack.
Tree-ring paleoclimate data proved Tidewater Virginia/North Carolina suffered its severest drought in 800 years during 1587–1589.
English-origin 16th-century artifacts have been recovered in both Hatteras Island and Bertie County ("Site X") excavations.

competingTheories.name: Dispersal & Assimilation with Croatoan & Inland Algonquian Communities
competingTheories.claim: Facing extreme drought and no ships, colonists split up and assimilated peacefully with Indigenous allies on Hatteras Island and inland rivers.
supportingEvidence: "CROATOAN" carving without cross, tree-ring drought data, Hatteras artifacts, and 1607 Jamestown accounts of assimilated Europeans.
competingTheories.scientificLimitations: No unambiguous 16th-century European cemetery or definitive DNA match yet discovered.

competingTheories.claim: All 115 colonists were killed in a raid or drowned trying to sail home.
supportingEvidence: Powhatan’s later contested 1608 claims to John Smith regarding another English group.
contradictingEvidence: Zero battle debris, burned structures, or distress cross at Fort Raleigh.
competingTheories.scientificLimitations: Evidence favors orderly departure.

scientificInvestigation.narrative: X-raying John White’s 1585 "La Virginea Pars" watercolor map revealed a hidden fort symbol patched over near Bertie County—guiding modern excavations inland.

whatRemainsUnknown: Genetic confirmation or skeletal burials tracing specific Roanoke descendants.
mysteries.finalAssessment: Rather than vanishing into thin air, Roanoke’s settlers almost certainly relocated to survive an epic drought—leaving behind archaeological footprints across coastal North Carolina.

mysteries.title: The Lost Patrol (RNWMP 1910–1911)
mysteries.subtitle: Four Royal North-West Mounted Police officers perished in a brutal Yukon blizzard
mysteries.summary: Setting out in December 1910 on the annual winter mail run from Fort McPherson to Dawson City, Inspector Francis Fitzgerald and three constables took a fatal shortcut—found frozen just miles from shelter.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: Unlike unresolved disappearances, the fate of the 1910–1911 Lost Patrol was verified in March 1911 when Corporal Dempster’s rescue party recovered all four bodies, Inspector Fitzgerald’s tragic diary, and his final pencil will.

overview.what: The winter 1910–1911 disappearance and recovery of Inspector Francis Fitzgerald’s four-man Royal North-West Mounted Police sled patrol in the subarctic Mackenzie Mountains.
overview.where: Between Fort McPherson (NWT) and Dawson City (Yukon), Canada.
overview.when: Departed December 21, 1910; bodies recovered March 21–22, 1911.
overview.narrative: Every winter, Mounties delivered mail over 760 km of frozen wilderness. That December, Fitzgerald decided to travel light on rations and brought a First Nations guide unfamiliar with the upper Peel River passes. When temperatures plunged below -50°C and blizzards buried landmarks, the men missed the crossing to Dawson, turned back starving, ate their sled dogs, and died within 40 km of Fort McPherson—leaving behind one of the most haunting diaries in Canadian history.

whyMysterious: Why did an experienced Arctic inspector ignore normal ration standards and dismiss a familiar local guide on a treacherous winter trail?

Extreme -52°C temperatures, deep un-broken snow, and missing the Hart River pass caused fatal exhaustion.
All four officers are buried together in Fort McPherson cemetery, inspiring annual RCMP memorial patrols.

mysteries.finalAssessment: The Lost Patrol is a verified Canadian historical tragedy whose mystery was solved by a brave 1911 rescue patrol and a heartbreaking pocket diary.

mysteries.subtitle: The 1872 ghost ship found adrift near the Azores with cargo and provisions intact

mysteries.evidenceRationale: The ship’s intact cargo, missing yawl/chronometer/papers, and 3.5 feet of bilge water are verified by the 1873 Gibraltar Vice-Admiralty Court transcripts, yet why Captain Benjamin Briggs ordered an emergency evacuation remains unresolved.

overview.what: A 282-ton American merchant brigantine discovered completely abandoned under partial sail on December 4, 1872 by the British brig Dei Gratia.
overview.where: Roughly 400 nautical miles east of the Azores in the North Atlantic.
overview.when: Last log entry November 25, 1872; found adrift December 4, 1872.
overview.narrative: Unlike Arthur Conan Doyle’s later fictional story ("J. Habakuk Jephson’s Statement")—which invented warm cups of tea and bloody swords—the real Gibraltar court records show a ship soaked from rough squalls, with 3.5 feet of water in the hold, one disassembled sounding pump, open cargo hatches, and a missing lifeboat. Nine barrels of denatured alcohol were empty, leading modern researchers to suggest sudden alcohol-vapor flashes or a clogged pump terrified Captain Briggs into ordering everyone into the lifeboat temporarily—until the towline snapped.

whyMysterious: What sudden alarm prompted a seasoned captain carrying his wife and two-year-old daughter to abandon a fundamentally seaworthy ship?

The ship’s chronometer, sextant, navigation book, and sole yawl (lifeboat) were all missing—showing an intentional, hasty evacuation.
Nine wooden barrels made of porous red oak (prone to leaking) were completely empty in the hold.

competingTheories.claim: Leaking denatured-alcohol fumes triggered a pressure flash blowing off the hatch, or coal-dust clogged pumps convinced Briggs the ship was sinking—prompting evacuation into the yawl.
supportingEvidence: Nine empty red-oak barrels, propped/displaced hatch covers, and disassembled pump rod on deck.
contradictingEvidence: No burn marks were recorded on deck timbers in Gibraltar.
competingTheories.scientificLimitations: Zero crew members ever survived to testify.

supportingEvidence: Popular Victorian speculation.
contradictingEvidence: Zero bloodstains, intact valuables/alcohol cargo, and careful removal of navigation instruments.
competingTheories.scientificLimitations: Refuted by Gibraltar forensic inspection.

scientificInvestigation.narrative: University College London chemistry demonstrations in 2006 showed alcohol vapor in an enclosed hold can create a terrifying pressure wave without scorching wood.

whatRemainsUnknown: Exact trigger behind Briggs’s evacuation order between November 25 and December 4, 1872.
mysteries.finalAssessment: The Mary Celeste crew almost certainly evacuated into their lifeboat in a sudden panic—only to be lost at sea while the sturdy brigantine sailed on unmanned.

overview.what: The 1483 disappearance of deposed boy-king Edward V (age 12) and Richard, Duke of York (age 9), inside the royal fortress of the Tower of London.
overview.where: Tower of London, England.
overview.when: Last reliably sighted mid-1483; children’s bones unearthed under a Tower staircase in 1674.
overview.narrative: In June 1483, Parliament declared the two boys illegitimate and crowned their uncle Richard III. Contemporary Italian observer Dominic Mancini wrote in December 1483 that the boys were moved deeper into the inner Tower apartments and seen less and less until rumors of their murder swept London. In 1674, workmen demolishing a staircase near the White Tower dug up a wooden chest holding two small skeletons—buried in Westminster Abbey by Charles II, where DNA testing has never yet been permitted.

whyMysterious: Why were no recognizable remains of five children found in the initial ash inspection—and why were ladders moved and trucks disabled that night?

mysteries.title: The Manhattan Project
mysteries.subtitle: The $2 billion secret wartime scientific enterprise that built the atomic bomb
mysteries.summary: Employing over 130,000 workers across hidden cities in Tennessee, Washington, and New Mexico—most without knowing what they were building—the Manhattan Project unleashed the nuclear age in July 1945.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: The Manhattan Project is one of the best-documented scientific-military undertakings in human history, verified by tens of thousands of declassified DOE, Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, and Hanford records.

overview.what: The top-secret Allied WWII research and industrial program (1942–1946) led by Gen. Leslie Groves and physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer to design and build the first nuclear weapons.
overview.where: Los Alamos (NM), Oak Ridge (TN), Hanford (WA), Chicago, and Chalk River.
overview.when: 1942–1946; Trinity Test detonated July 16, 1945.
overview.narrative: Fearing Nazi Germany would build an atomic weapon first, the U.S., UK, and Canada poured $2 billion (~$30+ billion today) into giant uranium-enrichment plants at Oak Ridge and plutonium reactors at Hanford while scientists at isolated Los Alamos solved implosion physics. Secrecy was so tight that even Vice President Harry Truman did not learn of the bomb until President Roosevelt’s death in April 1945.

whyMysterious: How did 130,000 ordinary engineers, clerks, and laborers operate massive nuclear cities for three years while hiding the secret from Congress, the press, and even the Vice President?

whatWeKnow: Soviet espionage (notably Klaus Fuchs and Ted Hall) penetrated Los Alamos early, accelerating the 1949 Soviet atomic test.
Only a tiny fraction of workers knew the end product—strict compartmentalization split every step.
Trinity fallout and downwind radiological impacts on New Mexico "Downwinders" remain actively studied and debated in health policy.

mysteries.title: Operation Sea-Spray
mysteries.subtitle: The 1950 U.S. Navy secret open-air biological dispersal test over San Francisco
mysteries.summary: For six days in September 1950, a U.S. Navy minesweeper sprayed aerosolized bacteria off the San Francisco coast to model bioweapon vulnerability—exposing 800,000 unwitting residents.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: Operation Sea-Spray is completely verified by 1977 U.S. Senate testimony and declassified U.S. Army biological warfare vulnerability reports.
mysteries.locationName: San Francisco Bay & Golden Gate Coast, California, USA

mysteries.imageAlt: Operation Sea-Spray — archival editorial visual plate

overview.what: A September 1950 covert military test dispersing Serratia marcescens and Bacillus globigii aerosols over San Francisco to measure how wind carries biological clouds over a major city.
overview.where: 2 miles offshore of San Francisco across 43 monitoring stations.
overview.when: September 20–27, 1950; publicly revealed in 1976–1977.
overview.narrative: Believing Serratia marcescens was a harmless bright-red tracer bacterium, Navy crews aerosolized 5,000 gallons from a minesweeper’s hoses into coastal fog drifting across San Francisco. Almost every resident inhaled millions of spores. Days later, 11 patients at Stanford University Hospital developed unusual Serratia urinary infections—one fatally (Edward Nevin)—causing doctors to publish a medical paper years before anyone learned the military had sprayed the city.

whyMysterious: How many similar open-air tracer dispersals occurred across other U.S. cities before Congress exposed Army testing in 1977?

whatWeKnow: Military documents proved nearly all 800,000 San Francisco residents inhaled ~5,000+ particles per minute during peak plumes.
The 1977 Senate inquiry revealed 239 open-air simulant tests across populated areas including New York subways and Minneapolis.
Edward Nevin’s family sued the government in 1981; courts acknowledged the test while ruling the government immune for discretionary defense decisions.

mysteries.title: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study
mysteries.subtitle: The 40-year U.S. Public Health Service study that withheld cure from 399 Black men
mysteries.summary: From 1932 to 1972, federal physicians deliberately left hundreds of Black sharecroppers in Alabama with untreated syphilis—even after penicillin became the standard cure in 1947.
mysteries.evidenceRationale: The 40-year Tuskegee Study, deceptive "bad blood" framing, active blocking of penicillin treatment, and 1972 whistleblower exposure are fully verified by CDC archives and the 1997 U.S. Presidential Apology.

overview.what: An unethical 40-year U.S. Public Health Service clinical study observing the natural course of untreated syphilis in 399 African American men alongside 201 uninfected controls.
overview.where: Macon County, Alabama.
overview.when: 1932–1972; exposed in July 1972 by whistleblower Peter Buxtun and reporter Jean Heller.
overview.narrative: Recruited with promises of free medical care for "bad blood," the men were never told they had syphilis and never gave informed consent. Even worse, when penicillin proved an effective cure in the mid-1940s, PHS researchers actively prevented participants from receiving antibiotics through local clinics or Army draft exams—continuing until whistleblower Peter Buxtun leaked the files to the Associated Press in 1972.

whyMysterious: How did dozens of physicians and public health officials publish open medical papers on this abuse for 40 years before public outrage forced its halt?

whatWeKnow: By 1972, 28 men had died directly of syphilis, 100 of related complications, 40 wives were infected, and 19 children were born with congenital syphilis.
It was NOT a "secret infection" study—men already had latent syphilis when enrolled, and the crime was deliberate deception and withholding of life-saving penicillin.
President Bill Clinton issued a formal national apology to survivors in May 1997.

overview.what: An anonymous internet horror story describing five WWII political prisoners sealed inside a gas chamber for 15 days without sleep.
overview.where: Purely fictional; originated online in 2009–2010.
overview.when: Posted online ca. 2009–2010; zero pre-2009 historical references.
overview.narrative: Often shared alongside a spooky Halloween-prop photo ("Spazm") to make it look like a real declassified Soviet dossier, the Soviet Sleep Experiment actually emerged from a creative-writing challenge on an online horror forum. Real sleep-deprivation science (such as Randy Gardner’s monitored 11-day awake record) produces micro-sleeps, hallucinations, and cognitive slowing—never superhuman strength or compulsive self-evisceration.

whyMysterious: Why do fictional internet horror stories paired with vintage-filtered photos so easily convince readers they are real Cold War history?

whatWeKnow: No Soviet military archive, Gulag record, or post-1991 Russian medical history mentions any 15-day stimulant gas chamber.
The famously scary black-and-white photograph circulated with the tale actually shows a commercial animatronic Halloween decoration named "Spazm."
Human biology forces involuntary micro-sleeps after 3–4 days regardless of stimulants.
